title: Wealth wrongly gathered and the heretic's false teaching
english: Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited out. I know another wealth gathered unjustly: the wealth in the words of the heretics, who hold teachings opposed to the doctrines of truth, the teachings they carry in their bellies. These teachings are not sweet, but are "the gall of an asp"—that is, evil—as it is said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses concerning the wine of their teaching: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 32:32). But the good God will not allow them to keep wealth gathered unjustly within themselves forever; he will make them vomit it out. For an angel, by God's kindness, will drag them out of the very house they built so badly—which is the church of those who do evil. So he adds: "Out of his house," and what follows.

Consider how much is stored up for the heretic because of his impious doctrines. For this reason let us watch ourselves, so that we are never robbed by persuasive speeches drawn from heretical teaching and fall away from the mystery of the Church. May he not see the milking of pastured souls. And the heretic does not see the milking of pastured souls. Pastured souls are souls nourished by the good shepherd, souls that have found pasture. And the doctrines against God have nothing sweet in them, but are harsh and dense. For he has shattered the houses of many powerless ones. And if the heretic finds you somewhere weak in faith, weak in sound teaching, he robs you by stealth. And it is truly possible to say of the teacher of heretics that he has shattered the houses of many powerless ones. He seizes the livelihood of the easily deceived one, and after that he does not establish it; for falsehood cannot be established. May a day of wrath come upon him—the day on which divine justice is stirred against him. Whether it is the circumcised man who has acted impiously toward God, or the heretic, or any impious person whatever, his portion is the one described in the words above.

Chapter 21. Why do the impious live, and grow old in wealth? Now the phrase "they grow old in wealth" he said instead of: they are not newly rich, but they have continued being rich from youth until old age. Taking up the psaltery and the lyre. There is another happiness of fathers: the joy of their children, which flutes and lyres and drums bring to fullness. By these their ears are played upon, the pleasures of the soul are stirred up, and those present are charmed by the licentious melody. The children of the impious produce this melody shamelessly, laying their hands on the stretched strings and beating time to the sound of the instruments. They finished their life amid good things. That is, there was no interruption of their prosperity, but they continued luxuriating in bodily goods through a complete life; and the end of their happiness was the end of their life, since their good fortune stretched out until death. And they slept in the rest of Hades. This means: resting and rejoicing until death, they go down to Hades untormented. Or it means that death itself does not become bitter for them, but they die as if falling asleep. Or it means that while others suffer and are afflicted in life, and rest after death, these people about whom the word speaks pass their whole life in cheerfulness, and so they come to the rest that is in death.

Chapter 22. Is it not the Lord who teaches? This doctrine is sound: that no human being can be the true teacher of virtue. For "he who teaches a human being knowledge" (Psalm 94:10; LXX 93:10) is also written in the Psalms, and it is no other than God. God teaches by shining into the soul of the one who learns from him, and by illuminating the mind with the true light through his own Word. Therefore, even if righteous men teach us, having received the grace of teaching, it is still the Lord who teaches us through them. And the very act of understanding and having our hearts opened to receive divine lessons happens according to divine grace. Or will he make an account of you and convict you? To this we might say: God does not convict the impious because he is worried that he himself might be harmed, but because he makes an account of the one under his providence and does good to him. You took pledges from your brothers for nothing. He supposes this about Job from the fact that he knew him to be rich, and suspected that he had become rich from such sources. Therefore he says: "You used to take pledges for nothing"—that is, when nothing was owed to you. And pressing further, he names another sin of his: You stripped the clothing of the naked. It is possible to take clothing not from a naked man, but from a rich man who has many garments stored away.

title: Eliphaz's accusations and Job's boldness
english: But if someone has a single tunic, and I strip that tunic from him on the pretext of demanding what is mine, without pitying the naked man, then I have taken away the clothing of the naked. Many such things happen among us when we lend money and when we have debtors. Often our debtor is extremely poor and cannot repay. We harden our hearts and do not see that he feeds a wife and children and barely feeds himself from the few small coins he earns, yet we demand payment bitterly, sometimes even while we have more than enough at home. So Eliphaz says this in accusing Job: "You took away the clothing of the naked" (Job 22:6). Perhaps he also calls the failure to give a garment to the naked an act of taking away, for the one who does not clothe the naked and the one who does not feed the one in need of bread is a robber and a greedy person.

"And you admired the faces of some" (Job 22:8). This is another sin, for admiring a face is also a sin. A certain person is rich, and I admire his face, but I trample down the poor man because he has no rank.

"So the Almighty will be your helper" (Job 22:25). Here Eliphaz speaks a sound doctrine, for he thinks Job suffers because of his sins, and that by enduring he will be purified through the suffering itself. And being purified, like gold in a furnace, he is shown to be genuine, having cast off everything foreign and become unmixed with every evil. He says, then, that if you also endure what has happened to you, God will give you back pure, like silver refined by fire. And when you have become pure, you will have boldness, since you have cast off your sins, and you will lift your face cheerfully to heaven, making your supplications with an uncondemned conscience, and so with boldness. And if you vow and promise anything to God, he himself will strengthen you to bring your promises to him to completion, for he is "the one working in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:13). Instead of "He will give you to repay your vows" (Job 22:27), Theodotion rendered it, "And you will determine a word, and it will be established for you," that is, whatever you arrange and set in order will not fail. To put it simply, he will provide you with the whole way of life that befits a righteous person, and all your paths will prosper, guided by the divine light; or your deeds will be bright and successful.

"Because he humbled himself, and you will say: He acted proudly" (Job 22:29). He seems to speak about someone else, but the word is directed at Job. For this reason, he says, these things will happen to the one who repents: because he humbled himself and said that he justly underwent what he suffered, since he had acted proudly. "And he will save the one who bows down with his eyes" (Job 22:29). That is, the humble-minded one, the one who looks down because of a troubled conscience and lack of boldness, like the tax collector who was justified in the Gospels.

Chapter 27. And Job, adding still more to his opening speech, said: The devil received authority over Job and tested him night and day, first through external things, then through his own body, and after these things also through his friends. For when he tested him through his wife and saw that Job had not been defeated, he brought three friends, not enemies, not men holding treacherous doctrines, but men with true words that were not offered well or at the right time. Through them he wanted to make the righteous man say something against Providence, to act impiously because of his pains, to lose heart because of his anguish. But this solid adamant, see what he says after the speeches of the three, when Eliphaz had finished three discourses, Bildad three, and Zophar two: "For I am not conscious of having done anything wrong" (Job 27:6). Paul later uttered this too, and added: "But I am not justified by this" (1 Corinthians 4:4). Great is the boldness of the righteous man, both concerning his former life and concerning the things at the time of his trial, so that he says: "I am conscious of nothing against myself."

Chapter 29. "And the mighty ceased speaking" (Job 29:9). Or according to the other Greek translations, "the rulers." These men, yielding the word to the righteous man, fell silent in his presence. "Putting a finger on their mouth" (Job 29:9). It may seem that putting a finger on the mouth is a sign of silence. But perhaps, since the hand is taken for deeds, it shows that their work muzzled their lips, and a kind of bond lay upon their mouth. For they perceived that they were not worthy to speak while Job was present, since he had done greater deeds while they had accomplished little. For the finger signifies the smallest action and activity.

"And I had put on righteousness" (Job 29:14). Job wove a beautiful tunic for himself, so that he might put on righteousness instead of a tunic. See also his cloak: righteousness is the tunic, judgment is the double cloak. Chapter 32. [The commentary on chapters 30–31 is lost.]

title: Elihu's speech: knowledge, birth of words, and God's night watches
english: Elihu says: “I was afraid to announce my own knowledge to you.” He does claim to have knowledge—or, according to the other Greek translations, understanding—of how people suffer in this life, and how some who are unjust flourish. I have seen people committing injustice and breaking the law, and yet thriving, and my feet were nearly shaken—if I look at this life alone; but if I consider what is to come, my feet stand firm. That is why he says: “Listen to me.”

Some manuscripts, after “For I will speak while you listen,” also have these lines: “Behold, I have heard your words, and I gave ear as far as your understanding went.” The other Greek translators have rendered it this way: “Behold, I have received your words; I listened as long as you were thinking, as long as you were examining words, and I understood until I reached you.” According to that version and those manuscripts, Elihu means this: Just as I listened in silence to everything you said, and waited until you finished your speeches, and until you emptied out all your own thinking, so you also listen to my words. But according to the manuscripts we use, the sense is this: “Listen to me,” he says, “for I will say nothing excessive, but only what you can test. And I will understand as far as you do.” That means: I will not use empty sounds, but I will speak in a way you can follow. Or he means this: I will not stop speaking before you test my words, to see whether I too can understand as far as you do—that is, as far as you can grasp—or whether I even surpass your understanding.

“For I am full of words” (Job 32:18). He was right to say “I am full.” For someone who is not full of words, and yet comes to speak, will speak empty things because he is empty, according to what is written: “For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will think empty thoughts” (Isaiah 32:6).

“The spirit of my belly destroys me.” Just as a woman becomes pregnant, and when the child is formed within her she comes to birth pangs until she gives birth to what she has conceived, so it also happens with a soul that loves learning. It conceives the word, and as it is announced it shapes it and forms it with order. When it has shaped and formed it and hands it over complete, then it gives birth. And until it gives birth, it is weighed down in birth pangs. “I will speak, so that I may find rest, opening my lips.” The person who has an intelligent hearer, and is full of words, finds rest in speaking, since he empties out and casts off his overflow.

Chapter 35. “Look up to the sky” (Job 35:5). The person who looks up to the sky is not the one who raises his bodily eyes and sees the sky; dogs and donkeys have that kind of looking up. No lover of the world looks up to the sky, but only the one who does not love the world or the things in the world. Again, the clouds are not as high above us as this: if I look at the life of Moses, and his pleasing of God, and my own smallness and lowliness, that is how I see the cloud high above me. If I come to Joshua son of Nun, to the lives of the prophets, if I examine their deeds, then I do what is written, and I learn how high the clouds are above me.

“If you have sinned, what will you do?” Elihu says: “Do you know, if you have sinned, what you will do to undo the sin?” If you have sinned in words, heal yourself with better words. If you have sinned in deeds, heal yourself with deeds that excel. But if your transgressions are many and incurable, then for the incurable things that we cannot heal ourselves, Jesus Christ came from heaven, so that he might heal the incurable, and so that it might be fulfilled: “Blessed are those whose sins are forgiven” (Psalm 32:1).

“The one who orders night watches” (Job 35:10). See how Elihu goes through praises and hymns of God, saying about him, “The one who orders night watches.” Do you want to see how God orders night watches? This whole age is night; it is darkness. The light is kept for you. For now you see through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12), but one day you will see the light. So this whole age is night, and there is need of guards appointed for this night, so that the guards, those on duty through the nights, may protect those who are in the night from robbers, from wild beasts, from enemies. Who are the guards? The angels who encamp around.

“The one who separates me from the four-footed creatures of the earth” (Job 35:11). According to the other Greek translators: “The one who teaches us beyond the beasts of the earth, and makes us wise beyond the birds that fly through the air.” For the human being alone has been honored with reason.
